CopyOnWriteArray wraps a (possibly backend/on-disk or shared) array and only copies it on the first write, via `_ensure_copied()`, which does `np.array(self.array)` and sets `_copied=True`. Reads and indexing never need a copy, so the copy is skipped unless a mutation actually happens. That avoids loading data or using memory for read-only use, and it protects the original from mutation. Every set path calls it first: `__setitem__`, `_oindex_set` and `_vindex_set`. Reads stay lazy: `__getitem__`, `_oindex_get` and `_vindex_get` return a new CopyOnWriteArray wrapping the lazily indexed result, so nothing is materialized. `__deepcopy__` also returns a new wrapper around the same underlying array without copying it, because the array may point to a file on disk.

A DataArrayRolling can only roll over dimensions that its array actually has. A data variable that lacks every rolling dimension has nothing to roll, and building a rolling object for it would fail or do nothing useful. So DatasetRolling.__init__ loops over the data variables and keeps only the dimensions in `self.dim` that the variable has. It also keeps the matching `center` values and window sizes. It creates a DataArrayRolling only if at least one such dimension exists (`if dims:`). Variables without a rolling dimension get no rolling object. `_dataset_implementation` handles them separately by copying them unchanged and clearing their attrs unless `keep_attrs` is set. The code comment says "keeps rollings only for the dataset depending on self.dim".

__post_init__ deep-copies the grouper because factorize() can mutate it. For example, BinGrouper.factorize() replaces BinGrouper.bins with the bin edges computed by pd.cut when `bins` was given as an int. Working on a copy leaves the user's original Grouper unmodified. The same grouper instance can then be reused across several groupby operations without carrying over state, such as the bin edges, from an earlier operation or from a different object.

In ResolvedGrouper.__post_init__, when the group variable is a chunked (e.g. dask) array, it raises ValueError in two cases. (1) UniqueGrouper with labels=None: the unique groups can only be found by scanning the data, which means computing the array. (2) BinGrouper with an integer `bins`: pd.cut needs the data's min and max to compute the bin edges, which also needs a pass over the data. Both would force an eager compute while xarray is building the graph, which breaks lazy evaluation. The user must pass explicit `labels` or explicit bin edges. Then the group structure is known up front and the data stays lazy. The checks are at lines 345-360 and the raise for the UniqueGrouper case is at line 350. The older check in groupers.py:208 gives the same constraint for UniqueGrouper.

The test goes through the grid_mapping formats in stages because grid_mapping can be written several ways, and the parser has to accept all of them (whats-new, issue 9761). It starts with the simple form "crs: x y". It then tries the extended form with several mappings, "crs: x y crs2: lat lon". Next it tries a stray colon, "crs2 : lat lon", which must still decode. Last, it tries a malformed value with a missing colon, "crs x y crs2: lat lon", which must raise ValueError matching "misses ':'". After that it deletes grid_mapping and moves on to formula_terms. That attribute also needs parsing (both are in CF_RELATED_DATA_NEEDS_PARSING). A valid value must decode, and a malformed value must only emit a UserWarning, "has malformed content". Each stage checks that the decoded coords set matches what is expected.

Each test in TestCombineMixedObjectsbyCoords builds its own small DataArray and Dataset inputs inline. These are the same few objects, such as named_da, unnamed_da and Dataset({"b": ("x", [2, 3])}), rebuilt in every method. Construction goes through coordinate and index creation, alignment and validation, so the repeated builds add overhead that grows with the number of tests. The objects are tiny, so the cost per test is small. The optimization is to move the common inputs into pytest fixtures or small factory helpers, e.g. a fixture or a setup method that returns fresh objects for each test. That removes the duplicated construction code while keeping isolation, because each test still gets its own objects. A wider-scoped fixture would build the objects once, but only if the tests never mutate them. combine_by_coords returns new objects and does not modify its inputs, so that is plausible. The class has no fixtures or setup today. I did not measure the actual time cost.

test_validating_attrs loops over three attribute scopes (dataset, variable "data", coordinate "y"). Before each of its ~7 scenarios it calls new_dataset_and_attrs(). That helper builds a new Dataset (np.arange data and a "y" coordinate) and returns the attrs dict to mutate. Each scenario needs a clean, un-mutated dataset, so it is rebuilt each time. That is about 3 scopes × 7 cases ≈ 20 identical Dataset constructions. Three wrapper functions that differ only in which attrs they return add more repetition.

Ways to reduce it while keeping all three scopes covered:
- Use @pytest.mark.parametrize over scope and (attr key/value, expected exception, match) cases. Each case then gets its own test id and one fixture-built dataset.
- Build one module-level or fixture dataset and call .copy(deep=True) per case. Deep copy duplicates attrs (see GH2835), so mutations don't leak between cases.
- Replace the three wrappers with one helper that takes a selector, such as lambda ds: ds.attrs, ds.data.attrs or ds.coords["y"].attrs.
- Skip the file write for the invalid cases. These cases raise in _validate_attrs, which to_netcdf calls in xarray/backends/api.py, so calling it directly avoids any I/O. Only the valid case needs a tmp file.

The dataset is tiny, so the real cost is mainly clarity and repetition rather than runtime.

Frozen is only a thin read-only view (a Mapping proxy) around an existing dict. In DataTreeCoordinates.variables, `Frozen(self._data._coord_variables)` allocates one small wrapper object per call and doesn't copy the Variable objects or their data. Every access goes through an extra level of indirection (`Frozen.__getitem__`, `__iter__` and `__len__` delegate to the wrapped mapping). Repeated calls therefore create short-lived wrapper garbage and add a little overhead per lookup, but they don't duplicate coordinate arrays. The cost is larger for DataTree.variables at datatree.py:702, `Frozen(self._data_variables | self._coord_variables)`. The `|` builds a new merged dict on every call, which is O(n) in the number of variables. The `dtypes` property at coordinates.py:867 also builds a new dict on every call.

Ways to reduce the overhead:
- Cache the Frozen view or the merged mapping, and invalidate it when the node changes.
- Hold the result in a local variable instead of calling `.variables` repeatedly.
- Look up single names directly with `node._coord_variables[name]`.
- Use a lazy ChainMap-style view instead of merging the dicts.
- Avoid building a merged dict when only the coordinate variables are needed.

The code doesn't document or measure a bottleneck for this sequence, so I can't confirm one. What it shows is that the three calls chain together, and the middle step creates variables. `Index.from_variables()` builds the index from the existing coordinate variables. `Coordinates.from_xindex(index)` then calls `index.create_variables()` to build the coordinate variables from scratch. It maps each variable name to the same index and returns a `Coordinates` object. `ds.assign_coords(coords)` then merges those variables and indexes into the dataset. The test branches because the reduction itself behaves differently by dtype. With skipna=False, a NaN in a float array propagates, so the min is the NaN element and the test expects the value at nanindex. Object-dtype arrays (kind "O") don't propagate NaN that way. With skipna=False they give the same result as the default skipna min, so the test expects expected1 (the min index) there. The same applies when there is no NaN (nanindex is None). The 2D test does the same per row: `x if y is None or ar.dtype.kind == "O" else y`. The test therefore mirrors the dtype-dependent NaN semantics of the underlying reductions. It does not apply one uniform rule. I only read the tests and did not read the reduction code in duck_array_ops. So the object-dtype explanation is inferred from the test's expectations.

ResolvedGrouper turns the abstract Grouper instruction into executable state: its docstring describes it as the concrete version holding the intermediates a GroupBy needs, and it gets those from `factorize`, which every Grouper must implement and which returns an `EncodedGroups` dataclass of "intermediate values for GroupBy operation." The `__post_init__` copy shows it also guards against mutating the user's grouper, since a grouper may be reused and `BinGrouper.factorize()` can update its bins.

In `_enforce_size_limit`, each loop iteration first removes the oldest entry with `self._cache.popitem(last=False)`. Only after that does it call `self._on_evict(key, value)`, and only if `_on_evict` is not None. So the entry is already gone from the cache when the callback receives the (key, value) pair. The callback is the last step in the entry's life in the cache. For FILE_CACHE it is `v.close()`, which closes the evicted file. If no callback is set, the entry is simply dropped. `popitem(last=False)` pops from the front of the OrderedDict, so eviction is FIFO over the cache's order, with the least recently used entry first. This works as LRU only because other code keeps that order current. `__setitem__` deletes and re-inserts an existing key to move it to the end, and `__getitem__` presumably does the same with `move_to_end`. The loop `while len(self._cache) > capacity` therefore evicts and runs callbacks in oldest-to-newest order until the size is within capacity. Callers hold `self._lock` while this runs, so the pop and the callback happen together.

In `DaskIndexingAdapter._vindex_get`, `dask.array.map_blocks` is called only when `self.array.vindex[indexer.tuple]` raises an IndexError. After that, the error is re-raised if any of these is true:
- No element of `indexer.tuple` is a dask array (`not has_dask`).
- `len(indexer.tuple) > 1`.
- `math.prod(self.array.numblocks) > 1`, meaning the array has more than one chunk.
- `self.array.ndim > 1`.

If none of those hold, there is a single indexer `idxr`, and two cases follow:
- If `idxr.ndim == 0`, it returns `self.array[idxr.data]`.
- Otherwise it calls `dask.array.map_blocks(_apply_vectorized_indexer_dask_wrapper, idxr[..., np.newaxis], self.array, chunks=idxr.chunks, drop_axis=-1, dtype=self.array.dtype)`.

The code comment says this path is meant for idxmin and idxmax on small 1D, single-chunk coordinate arrays.

In RenderDataTree.__next (xarray/xarray/core/datatree_render.py), the child-skipping condition is in the `for i, (child, is_last) in enumerate(_is_last(children))` loop. A child is rendered only if maxchildren is None, or i < ceil(maxchildren/2), or i >= ceil(nchildren - maxchildren/2). Children whose index falls between those two bounds are skipped. The first ceil(maxchildren/2) children and the last floor(maxchildren/2) children are kept, because ceil(n - m/2) = n - floor(m/2). The head and tail therefore sum to maxchildren, split symmetrically (the head gets the extra one when maxchildren is odd). A "..." row is yielded at i == ceil(maxchildren/2) when nchildren > maxchildren (lines 216-221).

In the test class's __init__, `self.__name__` is an instance access and raises a no-member error, because `__name__` is defined on the class object and not on its instances. The correct access is `self.__class__.__name__`. It goes through `__class__`, which every instance inherits from Python's base `object`, to reach the class, and the class carries `__name__`. So reading the class name from an instance depends on `__class__` being available on every object.

The cache stores each call's arguments together with its returned result, so the arguments act as the lookup key for the cached return value. Because of that link, the cache keeps the arguments alive indefinitely. For a method this includes `self`, which is never garbage collected. The checker message at this line states it: "the 'self' argument will be linked to the function and therefore never garbage collected". I found no code that describes the relationship more directly, so this answer is inferred from that message.

Only leading if/break statements are collected as candidates.

SphinxDirectives subclasses RegExFilter (itself a subclass of enchant's Filter). It inherits RegExFilter._skip, which returns bool(self._pattern.match(word)). The spelling checker can then pass these Filter subclasses to the tokenizer as a list of filters, with no changes to the enchant interface.

In `_check_in_slots`, which backs assigning-non-slot, a base class with no `__slots__` makes the checker return without checking. Every class in `klass.ancestors()` must define `__slots__`, except `Generic` and `object`. A subclass that defines `__slots__` or includes `__dict__` in its slots therefore gets no warning for assigning to a name outside its slots. Where all ancestors do use slots, a `__dict__` entry in the slots also allows any attribute name.

A property defined on a metaclass (Meta.values) is looked up on the class object itself, so Parent.values and subclasses like Child.values resolve to the property's returned list. Pylint should not warn on those. In standard class creation, a property on the class is just an unbound property object when accessed through the class. In Meta2, a metaclass method a_method is shadowed by the class's own property a_method. So Child2.a_method is the property object, and iterating it or testing membership correctly raises not-an-iterable and unsupported-membership-test.

copy.deepcopy calls `__deepcopy__(memo)` with a single argument (the memo dict) besides self. A version defined as `__deepcopy__(self, memo, other)` needs an extra required parameter that copy never passes. Pylint therefore flags it as unexpected-special-method-signature: "The special method '__deepcopy__' expects 1 param(s), 2 were given".

The formatter is `_format_option_value(optdict: OptionDict, value: Any) -> str` in pylint/utils/utils.py. It takes `value: Any` and dispatches on type with an if/elif chain. It handles py_version, list/tuple, dict, compiled regexps (anything with `.match`), "yn" options and whitespace-only strings. Anything else goes through `str(value)`.

To add validation and type checking without breaking existing callers, I would:
- Keep the signature and the `Any` input type.
- Validate `optdict` as a mapping. Validate `value` against `optdict["type"]` only for the known option types.
- Keep the final `str(value)` fallback for arbitrary objects.
- Report mismatches with a warning, not an exception. A hard failure would break callers that pass odd objects today.
- Optionally use `typing.overload`, or a dispatch table keyed on option type, for the typed paths.

The `TestChild` test class (a regression test for pylint issue #9814) subclasses `SlotsManipulationTest`, which has `__slots__ = ["a", "b", "c"]`. It then does `__slots__ += ["d", "e", "f"]`, so `__slots__` is an augmented assignment instead of a plain redefinition. The test only checks that the class checker handles this case without crashing and without emitting an unexpected message. Here is how the checker handles it:

- `_check_slots` first checks that `"__slots__"` is in `node.locals`. It then infers the value with `node.ilookup("__slots__")`.
- For each inferred slots value, it calls `_check_redefined_slots(node, slots, values)`.
- `_check_redefined_slots` builds `slots_names` from the child's own slots. It builds the ancestor slot names from `node.local_attr_ancestors("__slots__")`, calling `ancestor.slots()` on each ancestor.
- It intersects the two sets and emits `redefined-slots-in-subclass` if they overlap.

`Reference` is a template-method-style base class (an interface with default behaviour). It declares the query methods `references_table`, `references_column` and `references_index`, and the mutation methods `rename_table_references` and `rename_column_references`. `inhibit_post_migrate` is a stealth option of the `flush` command. It isn't exposed on the command line, and Django's internals pass it through `call_command`. `flush` reads it with `options.get("inhibit_post_migrate", False)`. Normally, after the tables are truncated, `flush` emits `post_migrate` so that apps can recreate their data, such as permissions and content types, as if the database had just been migrated. When the option is True, that emit is skipped (`if sql_list and not inhibit_post_migrate`). `flush` also skips the emit when the SQL list is empty.

Django's test framework (`TransactionTestCase._fixture_teardown`) sets it to True in two cases:
- `available_apps` is set, because only a subset of apps is being flushed.
- `serialized_rollback` is used and the connection has `_test_serialized_contents`. Skipping `post_migrate` stops the data it would recreate from colliding with the serialized data that gets loaded back, so that data isn't loaded twice.

Person (django/tests/m2o_recursive/models.py) has two nullable self-referential many-to-one foreign keys, `mother` and `father`. Each is declared as `ForeignKey("self", models.SET_NULL, null=True, related_name=...)`, with distinct reverse accessors `mothers_child_set` and `fathers_child_set`. The "self" reference lets rows point to other rows in the same table, so you can walk up the tree through `mother`/`father` and down through the reverse sets. The two distinct related_names stop the reverse accessors from clashing.

SET_NULL requires `null=True`. Deleting a parent therefore doesn't cascade-delete the children. It nulls their `mother`/`father` reference, so the child rows survive and the family graph can be partly orphaned. Roots (people with unknown parents) are valid, and the constraint allows an unlimited number of generations. The schema doesn't prevent cycles or self-parenting. Reading ancestors needs null checks, and traversal has to be done recursively or iteratively in application code.

It passes an empty string as content to HttpResponse.__init__ and then sets `_is_rendered = False`, so no rendering happens when the response is built. Rendering is deferred to `render()`. QuerySet.aggregate() just builds a dict of expressions (positional args get their default_alias as the key) and hands it to Query.get_aggregation(). That method returns an empty dict early when there are no aggregate expressions (`if not aggregate_exprs: return {}`). The result of aggregate() is always a dict mapping alias to value, so with nothing requested the natural result is an empty mapping. It does not return None, which would break the dict contract and force callers to check for None. It does not raise, because "no aggregates requested" is a valid no-op, and it also skips running a database query. This is separate from aggregates over empty querysets, which return None per alias (or the `default` value).

The Migration class only stores `dependencies` (and `run_before`) as data. MigrationLoader.build_graph resolves and validates them, and MigrationGraph orders them.

- `add_internal_dependencies` adds same-app dependencies first, so `__first__` lookups find the right root node.
- `add_external_dependencies` then handles cross-app dependencies. It calls `check_key`, which resolves `__first__` and `__latest__` and raises ValueError for an unknown app or an app with no migrations. It also adds `run_before` edges in reverse.
- Edges are added with `graph.add_dependency(..., skip_validation=True)`, which creates DummyNode placeholders for missing parents.
- `MigrationGraph.validate_consistency` then raises an error if any DummyNode is left, which means a dependency points to a migration that doesn't exist.
- Ordering comes from `forwards_plan` and `backwards_plan`, which both call `iterative_dfs`. The DFS is post-order: a node's parents are visited, in sorted order, before the node itself. Dependencies therefore come out before dependents. The backwards plan walks children instead of parents.

The cited line is `iterative_dfs` in graph.py, the DFS that produces the topological order.

It returns `len(self.initial)` when `self.initial` is set, and 0 otherwise.

This means validation of a bound formset relies on the submitted management form. The count is read from the POST data, not recomputed from the initial data. If that data is missing or tampered with, the management form fails validation. In that case `cleaned_data` has no `INITIAL_FORMS` entry, and Django handles this by treating the formset as invalid. Irreversibility is signalled by a dedicated exception, `IrreversibleError(RuntimeError)`, defined in `django/db/migrations/exceptions.py`. It sits in a flat hierarchy beside the other migration errors: AmbiguityError, BadMigrationError, CircularDependencyError and so on. `Migration.unapply()` checks each operation's `reversible` property in phase 1, before anything runs. If any operation is not reversible, it raises `IrreversibleError` ("Operation ... is not reversible"), so no rollback work is started. The pattern is delegation. The Migration asks each Operation whether it is reversible and later calls that operation's own `database_backwards`. This is polymorphic, Template-Method-like behaviour. Each operation decides for itself, and the migration is irreversible if any operation is.

Field.run_validators in django/forms/fields.py runs every validator in a try/except. For each ValidationError it calls hasattr(e, "code"), looks up e.code in self.error_messages, and rewrites e.message. It then calls errors.extend(e.error_list) to collect the errors, and raises one combined ValidationError at the end. Under high load, failing validators cost the most. Each failure builds an exception, unwinds the stack, runs the hasattr and dict lookups, and copies its error_list into the list. The combined ValidationError then re-wraps those errors. Because it does not stop at the first failure, a single invalid value triggers this work for every failing validator.

I did not benchmark this. The cost follows from reading the code.

Refactoring that would improve throughput:
- Skip the hasattr check. ValidationError always has a `code` attribute (it may be None), so use `getattr(e, "code", None)` once and reuse it.
- Precompute or cache the error_messages override lookup instead of repeating it per exception.
- Collect errors lazily: append the exception's error_list only when it exists, and avoid building a new ValidationError when there is a single error. Re-raise that one error directly.
- Add an optional fail-fast mode that stops at the first error.
- Have validators return error results instead of raising for common checks, so the hot path avoids exception overhead.

The same pattern appears in django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:782 (model Field.run_validators), so the fix applies there too.

The code doesn't show a regression in clean() itself. Field.clean() at django/django/forms/fields.py:200 calls to_python(), validate() and run_validators() in a fixed order. Each step needs the previous step's output: to_python() produces the value, validate() checks it (for example the required check), and run_validators() runs every validator on it. The cost is linear per value: run_validators() loops over all validators and collects errors instead of stopping at the first one. It also returns early for empty values. With large datasets, that per-value work is repeated for every field of every form, and the cost is that repetition, not a bug in clean(). To optimize:
- Keep the validators list short.
- Make to_python() and the validators cheap.
- Avoid per-row queries inside validators.
- Validate in bulk, or skip the form layer for trusted data.
- Cache expensive lookups.

Field exposes several attributes through descriptors instead of plain instance attributes. `unique` is a `cached_property`. `db_tablespace` and `db_returning` are plain `@property`s that recompute on every access: `db_tablespace` reads `settings.DEFAULT_INDEX_TABLESPACE`, and `db_returning` calls `has_db_default()` and checks `connection.features`. `get_default()` goes through `_get_default`, a `cached_property` that returns a lambda or callable. `error_messages` and `validators` are also lazy `cached_property`s.

Each access costs a descriptor call and, for the plain properties, a recomputation. The first access to a `cached_property` also runs its function and stores the result in `__dict__`. Each one is small, but ORM operations read them millions of times, so the cost adds up.

To optimize, compute the values once, for example in `__init__` or `set_attributes_from_name`, and store them as plain attributes. Alternatively, convert the plain `@property`s to `cached_property`. Hot loops can also read the attribute once into a local variable.

MaskedInfoBase (astropy/utils/masked/core.py) doesn't pick a serialization strategy through subclassing. When an info object is bound, it gives each instance a `serialize_method` dict keyed by format (fits/ecsv → "null_value", hdf5/parquet → "data_mask", None → "null_value"). The `serialize_method_as` context manager in astropy/table/info.py temporarily overrides those per-instance values, and it is used only within Table.write. Trade-offs:
- Flexibility: the strategy can be chosen per write call, per format, per column name or per class, without defining new subclasses.
- Restoration: the override is scoped and temporary, so the defaults come back afterwards.
- Cost of the dict approach: the strategy is a string-keyed dict looked up at runtime, so there is no static or type-level guarantee and bad keys are caught late.
- Mutable state: the dict is shared mutable state on each bound instance, so overrides are not thread-safe.
- Discoverability: the behaviour is harder to find than an overridden method, because the defaults sit in one class and the overrides sit in another module.

TimeDeltaQuantityString (quantity_str) doesn't store its own value. Like all astropy Time/TimeDelta formats, it keeps the interval internally as two doubles, jd1 and jd2, whose sum is the Julian Date. A single float64 can't hold a long time span to sub-microsecond or nanosecond precision. Splitting it into a large part and a small part keeps the full precision.

`set_jds` follows this. It puts the whole days, `yrs*365.25 + days`, into jd1, which is exact when yr and d are integers. It puts the hours, minutes and seconds into jd2 as a fraction of a day, which is inexact. `day_frac(jd1, jd2)` then normalizes the pair into an integer day part and a fractional part. As the docs say, users who need only microsecond precision over about 100 years can ignore this representation.

Views share one `_id_cache`, which is a `WeakValueDictionary` mapping `id(instance)` to each Time instance that shares the data. Deleting `cache` (for example when an item is set) loops over every instance in that shared dictionary and clears each one's cache. Because the dictionary holds only weak references, no strong reference cycle forms between a Time and its slices. A deleted slice therefore gets garbage collected and drops out of `_id_cache`, and the original's cache is unaffected. The test checks this: after `del t01` and `gc.collect()`, `set(t._id_cache) == {id(t)}`.

The `cache` flag (default True) in `Convolution.__init__` decides whether the precomputed convolution is kept. When it is on, `_get_convolution` stores the interpolator over the whole bounding-box domain, plus the kwargs it was built with, in `self._convolution` and `self._kwargs`. Later calls with the same kwargs reuse it and skip recomputing, which saves computation but holds the full grid and interpolator in memory. When `cache` is off, nothing is stored, so each call rebuilds the grid, runs the convolution and builds a new `RegularGridInterpolator`. That uses less memory but costs more computation. The grid comes from `bounding_box.domain(self._resolution)`, so a larger step size gives a coarser, smaller grid and a smaller cache. A smaller step size gives a finer grid, more points, and a larger cache and a more expensive rebuild. Note that the code never changes `_resolution` itself. If it were changed at runtime, the cache would not be invalidated automatically, because the cache check compares only the kwargs. You would have to call `clear_cache()` to force a rebuild.

Cylindrical sets `_separable = True`, which marks the model as separable, meaning each output depends only on its own input (for example, longitude and latitude are transformed independently). This is `Table.__getstate__`. It keeps `BaseColumn` instances (`Column`, `MaskedColumn`) as they are and calls the mixin-safe `col_copy` only on other columns, meaning mixins. The code has no comment explaining this, so the following is my reading of it. `BaseColumn` pickles itself, so it needs no extra copy. A mixin may not have a plain `.copy()` method, and its `info` and indices need special handling. `col_copy` handles that: it uses `col.copy()` if the column has one and falls back to `deepcopy` otherwise. It also carries over `col.info` and re-points any indices at the new column. `col_copy` itself starts with `if isinstance(col, BaseColumn): return col.copy()`, so the conditional in `__getstate__` skips that copy for `BaseColumn` instances.

The code has no comment or benchmark that quantifies this overhead, so I can only describe where it comes from. `_validate_arg_value` runs on every call of a decorated function, for every argument that has unit targets. Each time, it calls `_get_allowed_units(targets)`, which rebuilds the `Unit` objects (or physical-type units) from the targets. It then makes repeated `hasattr(arg, "unit")` lookups. Inside the loop over allowed units it looks up `arg.unit` and calls `.is_equivalent(allowed_unit, equivalencies=...)` once per allowed unit. Nothing is cached between calls, so this cost is paid on every call in high-frequency use.
